summary: Learners build the idea that a cross-section is a NEW surface created where a slicing plane meets a solid, so its shape depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid. Core work is predict-then-slice on real solids (play-doh, carrot, food) at parallel, perpendicular and oblique orientations, naming the cut as distinct from any outer face the solid already had, scaffolding straight cuts before slanted ones, transferring the idea to a new solid such as a cone, counting faces/edges/vertices on the solid handled in the round, and linking a prism's constant cross-section to area-of-base-times-height.
misconceptions: A solid has one fixed cross-section — a cylinder is 'always a circle' whatever the slice.
Confuses the cross-section with a pre-existing outer face, reporting a surface the solid already had.
Assumes a 2-D shape extends orthogonally into 3-D, so a slanted cut of a cylinder is judged a circle rather than an ellipse (over-applying 'the slice looks like the base').
Counts only the faces and edges visible in a 2-D drawing, missing hidden ones.

activities.title: Predict, then slice: a cylinder gives more than a circle
steps: Hold a play-doh or carrot cylinder and a plastic knife.
BEFORE cutting, predict AND justify the shape of a straight top-to-bottom slice through the middle; write or say the reason.

Cut and compare the fresh cut face to your prediction (for a true cylinder a rectangle appears, not a circle; a real carrot that tapers gives a near-trapezium, an approximation to the ideal rectangle).
Make a second cut parallel to the circular ends and check that this one does give a circle.
State in your own words why the two cuts give different shapes.
activities.insight: A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so one solid yields many cross-sections depending on how it is sliced; a cylinder is only 'a circle' when sliced parallel to its base.

activities.title: Tilt the cut: straight before slanted
steps: After solving the parallel and perpendicular cuts, tilt the knife and cut the cylinder at a slant.
Predict first: is the slanted cut face still a circle? Name the shape you expect.
Cut, then lay the slanted cut face over a traced circle of the same cylinder to compare.

Describe how the oblique cut stretches the circle into an ellipse when the slanted plane crosses only the curved surface. If your cut also runs through a flat end, the face is part of an ellipse with a straight edge, so note which case you got.
Transfer the idea to a new solid: predict then check the cross-section of a cone sliced vertically through its apex (a triangle), to test slice-dependence on a different shape.
activities.insight: Assuming a 2-D shape extends straight up into 3-D leads to calling a slanted cut a circle; oblique cuts need more careful reasoning than straight ones, a slanted slice of a cylinder that crosses only the curved surface is an ellipse (one that also cuts an end is an ellipse cut off by a straight edge), and the slice-dependence idea transfers to other solids such as a cone.

activities.title: The sweep that makes a prism
steps: Take a triangular prism (or model one in play-doh).
Slice it parallel to its triangular end, then slice again further along its length.
Compare the cut faces: check whether the cross-section ever changes along the length.
Explain why a polygonal cross-section that never changes (for slices parallel to the end) is what makes the solid a prism, and connect this to volume as area of the end (base) times the length.
activities.insight: A prism is a constant polygonal cross-section swept along its length; this constancy (which a cylinder shares, with a circle as its cross-section) links the solid's properties to volume = area of base x height.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices in the round
steps: Hold the actual solid (triangular prism, square-based pyramid) and turn it over in your hands.
Count faces, edges and vertices, marking each face as you tally it so you do not miss hidden ones.
Compare your in-the-round count with what you would have counted from a flat 2-D picture of the same solid.
State how many elements the drawing would have hidden.
activities.insight: Counting from the solid handled in the round includes hidden faces, edges and vertices that a 2-D drawing conceals, so property-based reasoning must override the 'look' of a diagram.

activities.title: Explore slicing on a rotatable 3-D model (optional scaffold)
steps: On a 3-D model, grab a translucent cylinder and a rotatable slicing plane.
Rotate the plane from flat (parallel) to upright (perpendicular) to a slant, watching the cut face render in real time.

Observe how the cut face changes continuously as the plane tilts. Going from flat to upright, the circle stretches into ellipses, then into ellipses cut off by straight edges once the plane meets the ends, and finally becomes a rectangle when the plane is upright.
Keeping the plane parallel to the prism's end, sweep it along the prism's length and watch the cross-section stay constant.
activities.insight: Seeing the cut face morph continuously as a plane tilts makes the slice-dependence vivid: one solid, many cross-sections, the shape tracking the tilt of the plane.

checkQuestion: A solid cylinder — like a tin of beans — is cut straight across, parallel to its circular ends: what 2-D shape is the freshly cut face? Now the same cylinder is cut straight down through the middle, from top to bottom: what shape is that cut face? Explain why the two cuts give different shapes.
checkAnswer: The parallel cut gives a circle; the top-to-bottom (perpendicular) cut gives a rectangle. A cross-section is the shape where the slicing plane meets the solid, so it depends on the direction of the cut, not just on the solid — the cylinder is not 'a circle' by nature, only when sliced parallel to its base.
